title: HR Attendance Policy: What to Include + Template
summary: Build an HR attendance policy that holds up: what to include, no-call/no-show rules, FMLA, a template, and how to track it.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR**


- A good HR attendance policy defines schedules, lateness, absence reporting, no-call/no-show, leave, and consequences in plain language.
- Points-based systems are common but risky. Protected leave can never count against an employee.
- A policy works only if people read it. Collect signed or acknowledged copies and keep a record.
- Attendance records and the policy are separate jobs. Tools can track time, but a human still decides what counts as excused.


## **What an HR attendance policy actually does**


An attendance policy is a written set of expectations: when people work, how they report absences, and what happens when they don't meet them.


It is not a deterrent. No policy stops people from getting sick. What it does is give managers one consistent standard, so two people in the same situation get the same outcome. Inconsistent enforcement is where most attendance disputes come from, and it is usually a bigger legal problem than the policy's content.


## **What to include in an employee attendance policy**


Cover these eight elements, in plain language:


1. **Scope.** Who the policy applies to: full-time, part-time, hourly, salaried. Note whether contractors are covered. Contractors usually shouldn't be managed under an attendance policy, so review[when to hire independent contractors](https://warp.co/blog/when-should-startups-hire-independent-contractors) before applying it to them.
2. **Schedules and core hours.** Standard hours, remote or hybrid expectations, and any hours where availability is required.
3. **Lateness and early departure.** Define what counts as late (for example, more than 10 minutes after the scheduled start) and who to notify.
4. **Absence reporting.** Who to tell, how to tell them, and when to tell them. "As early as possible, and before your shift starts" is much better than just "reasonable notice."
5. **No-call/no-show.** A specific definition and a specific consequence.
6. **Leave and accommodations.** Point to your PTO, sick leave, FMLA, and accommodation processes, and be clear that protected absences are handled separately. Your[PTO policy](https://warp.co/blog/pto-policy-employer-guide-2026) and attendance policy should never contradict each other.
7. **Documentation.** When a doctor's note is requested, if ever. Check state rules first, because some states restrict it.
8. **Consequences.** Use a progressive path, such as a verbal conversation, written warning, final warning, then termination, and clearly state that management can skip steps for serious violations.


## **No call, no show policy: write it before you need it**


A no-call/no-show means an employee misses a shift or workday without notifying anyone. It is the most common trigger for termination under an attendance policy, so define it tightly.


State clearly how many consecutive missed days count as job abandonment (many employers use three; some use one for shift-critical roles). Say what a manager should attempt before acting: calls, texts, an email, and an emergency contact if appropriate. Then add the caveat: if the employee later shows the absence was due to an emergency or a protected reason, HR will review it before any final decision.


That last step matters. A person in a hospital cannot call in, and terminating them for it turns a routine policy into a legal claim.


## **Points-based vs. flexible attendance policies**


A **points-based (no-fault) attendance policy** assigns points per occurrence regardless of reason, with set consequences at thresholds. For example: late arrival is half a point, an unexcused absence is one point, a no-call/no-show is three points, and a written warning triggers at five. Points roll off after a set period of clean attendance.


The appeal is consistency and simplicity for managers. These policies generally work by accumulating points or occurrences for missed work or late arrivals, and workers can face discipline up to termination once they pass a threshold.


The risk is that "regardless of reason" is exactly what the law does not allow for protected absences. A **flexible, manager-discretion policy** avoids that trap but invites inconsistency. For most startups and small businesses under 100 people, a middle path works best: clear expectations, a progressive discipline ladder, and written guidance on which absences are never counted.


## **Legal traps in an attendance policy**


This is where most downloadable templates fall short. Check these before you publish:


- **FMLA.** Employers covered by the FMLA, generally those with 50 or more employees, cannot count FMLA leave against employees. Under the regulation, employers cannot count FMLA leave under no-fault attendance policies, so employees cannot accrue points for it. The Department of Labor has also said no-fault policies are generally acceptable as long as employers do not assess points for FMLA absences.
- **ADA and accommodations.** If an absence is tied to a disability or a pregnancy-related condition, discipline can create liability even if the policy is neutral on paper. Route those cases to HR before applying points.
- **State and local paid sick leave.** No federal paid sick leave law exists, but a growing number of states have their own. Either way,[all state sick leave laws prohibit retaliation](https://www.hivedesk.com/blog/paid-sick-leave-laws-in-the-us) against employees who use or request sick leave. Sick leave rules follow the employee's work location, not your headquarters, which matters for remote and multi-state teams.
- **Exempt employees.** Docking salaried exempt employees for partial-day absences can threaten their exempt status. Handle exempt attendance through performance management and leave balances, and confirm the approach with employment counsel.
- **Consistency.** Apply the policy consistently to everyone. Document each decision.


This is general information, not legal advice. Attendance rules vary by state, city, and company size, so have counsel review the final policy.


## **Attendance policy template**


Adapt this to your company. Plain language is a feature, not a shortcut.


### Attendance Policy


**Purpose.** \[Company\] relies on every team member to be present and reachable during scheduled hours. This policy explains what we expect and how we handle exceptions.


**Scope.** This policy applies to all \[employees / hourly employees / specify\].


**Schedules.** Your manager will confirm your schedule, including core hours of \[time range, time zone\].


**Lateness.** Arriving more than \[10\] minutes after your scheduled start without notice is considered late. Please message \[manager/channel\] as soon as you know you will be late.


**Reporting an absence.** Notify \[manager\] by \[phone/Slack/text\] before your scheduled start, or as soon as possible in an emergency.


**No-call/no-show.** Missing a scheduled shift or workday without notifying us is a no-call/no-show. \[Three\] consecutive no-call/no-show days may be treated as voluntary resignation after we have made reasonable attempts to reach you. If you could not contact us because of an emergency or protected reason, HR will review before any final decision.


**Protected leave.** Absences protected by law, including FMLA leave, approved accommodations, and protected sick leave, are handled under their own policies and are never counted as attendance violations.


**Consequences.** Attendance concerns are addressed through a progressive process: conversation, written warning, final warning, and termination. \[Company\] may skip steps for serious or repeated violations.


**Questions.** Contact \[HR contact\].


## **How to publish and track your attendance policy in Warp**


Writing the policy is half the job. The other half is proving people received it. In Warp's Training area:


1. **Create company-authored content or upload the policy as a PDF.**
2. **Cover the essentials:** schedules, lateness, absence reporting, no-call/no-show, leave and accommodations, and consequences.
3. **Choose Signature required or a read acknowledgment.**
4. **Assign it to the relevant employees or contractors and set a due date.**
5. **Turn on new-hire assignment if needed,** with a due-date offset from 1 to 365 days after hire.
6. **Monitor signatures, completion timestamps, and reminders** in completion reporting.


Two details make this useful over time. Warp preserves existing assignment history when you later change the audience rules for future hires, and policy versioning lets you send out a revised policy without erasing earlier acknowledgments. That gives you a clean record of who accepted which version, and when.


## **How can I track attendance in Warp?**


Use Warp's[Time Tracking](https://www.warp.co/time-tracking) feature to capture worked time and spot patterns like missed time, late starts, or incomplete entries. Workers record their time, and managers review the resulting timesheets alongside approved time-off records before payroll. Time Tracking may need to be enabled for your company.


One boundary to be clear about: Warp does not automatically decide whether an absence is excused, and it does not apply attendance points or trigger discipline. You compare time records against your attendance policy and handle exceptions through your own HR process. That is deliberate. Excused versus unexcused is a judgment call with legal weight, and it should stay with a person.


## **Frequently asked questions**


### What is a reasonable attendance policy?


One that sets clear schedule expectations, explains how to report absences, defines no-call/no-show, and carves out legally protected leave. Reasonable also means applied consistently to everyone.


### How many absences trigger HR?


There is no legal number. Most employers pick an internal trigger, such as a pattern of repeated unplanned absences within a rolling period, and review each case against protected leave before taking action. Write the trigger into your policy.


### Can I fire someone for a no-call/no-show?


Often yes, but follow your written policy and check for an emergency or protected reason first. Many employers define job abandonment as multiple consecutive no-call/no-show days. Have counsel confirm the approach for your state.
